To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Priming of SOM mineralization is an important process for both C and N cycling in forest soils.

priming is driven by stoichiometric imbalance between C and N, and by plant and microbial demands for nutrients, and that the priming response is a result of stimulated enzyme activity, rather than an increase in the concentration of extracellular enzymes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of elevated CO2 and nitrogen deposition on soil carbon and nitrogen mineralisation.
the role of plants and their root exudates in regulating the decomposition of soil organic matter.
the effect of environmental factors on the decomposition of soil organic matter, which in turn influences carbon sequestration and climate feedbacks in forest ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

priming is regulated by a combination of factors, including stoichiometric imbalances, plant nutrient demands, and microbial response to nutrient limitation, which all together determine the activity of oxidative enzymes.
priming is regulated by a combination of C and N availability, plant and microbial C and N demand, microbial C and N sequestration, and the microbial ability to decompose complex SOM components.
priming is an important process in forest soils, and that it should be included in global C and N cycling models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
priming is not just an effect of root exuded carbon, but a response to a C:N imbalance, which is regulated by plant and microbial physiology and stoichiometry.
priming of SOM decomposition is regulated by the balance between C and N availability in soil and the microbial response towards nutrient deficiency.

the priming effect is a complex process, and that we need to understand more about the mechanisms involved to be able to predict the effect that global changes will have on SOM decomposition and C cycling.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the microbial decomposition of soil organic matter is a key factor regulating the global carbon cycle, and that priming is an important process that needs to be accounted in order to accurately predict the effects of environmental changes such a elevated CO2 and increasing N deposition on C cycling in forest ecosystems.
the microbial decomposition of organic matter is not only regulated by the availability of carbon and nutrients, but also by microbial stoichiometric imbalances.
RPE is a key process in the global C cycle, and that it is of major importance to consider RPE when evaluating the effect of elevated CO2 and nitrogen deposition on terrestrial C sequestation.
